explanations.answer: Take a census of Israel and Judah
explanations.explanation: A census it is. The LORD says to David, Israel's king, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.” Counting heads sounds like the most harmless chore in the world. But this one has some weight to it, so stay close, friend.

explanations.answer: Go to war against the Moabites
explanations.explanation: No battle plans in this order, friend. The LORD tells David, Israel's king, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.” No swords drawn, no armor, just a head count. I know it's less exciting than a war, but that's what the text says.

The ark isn't part of this order. The LORD tells David, Israel's king, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.” It's a count of the people, nothing to do with carrying anything holy anywhere. Easy one to mix up when you've got a lot of David stories floating around in your head.

Number is the word. David says he wants Joab to register the troops “so that I may know their number.” He's after a total, plain and simple. I double-check my cookie boxes before I seal them, but David is trying to count a whole nation's worth.
Close, but leaders isn't what David asks for. His words are “so that I may know their number.” He wants a total of the troops, not a list of who's in charge. The word is number.

Homes aren't on David's mind here. He tells Joab to register the troops “so that I may know their number.” The goal is a total of the troops, not a map of where everybody lives. The missing word is number.

Joab does have a question, friend. Joab, the commander of David's army, says, “But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?” (2 Samuel 24:3). He asks right out loud, in front of the king. So the statement is false: he doesn't go along quietly.

False is right, and Joab is the reason. Joab, the commander of David's army, says, “But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?” (2 Samuel 24:3). He's the one in the meeting who asks, "Are we sure about this?" I think everybody needs a Joab around, even when the boss doesn't love the question.

The king's word wins. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army.” (2 Samuel 24:4). Joab and the commanders push back, and it still doesn't change the order. Outnumbered and the king still gets his way.

Joab speaks up, but his word doesn't win. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army.” (2 Samuel 24:4). So Joab and the commanders leave to register the troops. His question gets asked, and the king's word is still the one that stands.

The commanders are in the pushback, but they don't win it. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army.” (2 Samuel 24:4). So it's the king's word that carries the day. Joab and the commanders then depart to register the troops.

Nine months and twenty days, right on the nose. The text says, “At the end of nine months and twenty days, having gone through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem.” That's almost ten months on the road. A batch of cookies takes me one afternoon, so this is a different kind of job.

That's a lot shorter than the text says. The count took nine months and twenty days, and then they returned to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 24:8). They went through the whole land, and that took a good long while. Almost ten months of travel, friend.

That's longer than the text says. It reads, “At the end of nine months and twenty days, having gone through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem.” So it's nine months and twenty days, not a year and a half. Still plenty of time to wear out a pair of sandals.

True. The text says, “After David had numbered the troops, his conscience was stricken and he said to the LORD, ‘I have sinned greatly in what I have done.’” He speaks to the LORD about it himself. Gad hasn't even shown up yet at that point.

It's actually true, friend. After the count, “his conscience was stricken,” and David says to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done.” (2 Samuel 24:10). He says it before the prophet Gad arrives in the next verse. So David doesn't stay quiet about it.

Foolishly is the word. David says, “Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.” He doesn't dress it up or pass it along. He puts it plainly to the LORD and asks Him to take it away.

Wisely would be quite the plot twist, friend. But David says the opposite: “I have acted very foolishly.” (2 Samuel 24:10). He's not defending what he did. He's asking the LORD to take away his iniquity.
Boldly is a fun guess, but David doesn't use it. He says, “I have acted very foolishly.” (2 Samuel 24:10). He's not bragging about it. He's begging the LORD to take away the iniquity of His servant.

Three options, friend. Gad, David's prophet and seer, brings the LORD's words: “I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.” (2 Samuel 24:12). David gets to choose, and the LORD will carry out the one he picks. That's a weighty menu.

Two would make for an easier choice, but the text says three. Gad, David's prophet and seer, brings the LORD's words: “I am offering you three options.” (2 Samuel 24:12). Then David is to pick one. Three it is.

Seven would be a long list, but the text says three. Gad, David's prophet and seer, brings the LORD's words: “I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.” (2 Samuel 24:12). One pick out of three. Gad lays them out in the next verse.

That's the reason David gives. He says, “…for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.” (2 Samuel 24:14). Look at where he puts his hope. He'd rather land in the LORD's hand than anyone else's.

David doesn't say that. His reason is, “…for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.” (2 Samuel 24:14). He never says a word about how strong his enemies are. His eyes are on the LORD's mercies.

David doesn't mention his army here. He says, “…for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.” (2 Samuel 24:14). His reason is the LORD's mercies. That's where he wants to land.

It goes the other way, friend. The LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” (2 Samuel 24:16). The angel stretches out his hand toward Jerusalem, and the LORD stops him. So the statement is false.

False is right. The angel stretches out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, but “the LORD relented from the calamity” and said, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” (2 Samuel 24:16). The LORD stops him before it happens. I think that's a moment to breathe out.

explanations.answer: By the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite
explanations.explanation: That's the spot. The text says, “At that time the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:16). Araunah, a Jebusite, owns that threshing floor. Keep that place in mind, because it matters a lot in the next verses.

explanations.answer: By the well at the gate of Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: No well in this verse, friend. The text says the angel of the LORD was “by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:16). Araunah is a Jebusite, and the threshing floor is his. Bethlehem isn't mentioned here.

explanations.answer: By the great pool in Gibeon
explanations.explanation: No pool here. The text says the angel of the LORD was “by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:16). Araunah is a Jebusite, and the threshing floor is his. Gibeon isn't in this verse.

explanations.answer: Let His hand fall on David and his father's house
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks. David says, “Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.” (2 Samuel 24:17). The shepherd steps in front of the sheep. I think this one hurts a little to read.

explanations.answer: Spare David and his father's house
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what David asks. He says, “Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.” (2 Samuel 24:17). He doesn't ask to be spared. He asks the LORD to turn it toward himself and his family.

explanations.answer: Let His hand fall on the army commanders
explanations.explanation: The commanders aren't in David's request. He says, “Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.” (2 Samuel 24:17). He points at himself, not at anyone else. The shepherd takes the weight on his own side.

An altar is right. Gad, David's prophet and seer, says, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:18). The instruction comes the same day David speaks to the LORD. Nothing fancy, just an altar.

No house for the ark in this chapter. Gad, David's prophet and seer, says, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:18). It's an altar, and it's built on that threshing floor.

Nobody's building a watchtower here. Gad, David's prophet and seer, says, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (2 Samuel 24:18). No guard duty in this scene, just an altar.

Joab isn't in this scene at all. The text says, “So David went up at the word of Gad, just as the LORD had commanded.” (2 Samuel 24:19). David goes himself, and Araunah sees “the king and his servants coming toward him” (2 Samuel 24:20). No stand-in and no "have my people call your people."

False is right. The text says, “So David went up at the word of Gad, just as the LORD had commanded.” (2 Samuel 24:19). The king walks up there himself. Araunah sees “the king and his servants coming toward him” (2 Samuel 24:20).

Buying is the plan. David answers Araunah, “To buy your threshing floor… that I may build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague upon the people may be halted.” (2 Samuel 24:21). He says it straight to Araunah's face. No hints, no games.

Another count? That's not what David says. He tells Araunah, “To buy your threshing floor… that I may build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague upon the people may be halted.” (2 Samuel 24:21). He's there to buy, not to count.

David isn't there to collect anything. He tells Araunah, “To buy your threshing floor… that I may build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague upon the people may be halted.” (2 Samuel 24:21). The king is there to buy.
True. Araunah offers it all to the king, but David says, “No… I insist on paying a price.” (2 Samuel 24:24). Araunah gives and David refuses to take it free. Two men, both trying to be generous.

It's actually true, friend. Araunah gives everything to the king, and David replies, “No… I insist on paying a price.” (2 Samuel 24:24). He turns down the gift. Then he buys the threshing floor and the oxen.

Nothing is the word. David says, “…I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” (2 Samuel 24:24). It's a gift that costs him something. He's not about to hand over a free one.

Everything would be one steep price tag. David says, “…I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” (2 Samuel 24:24). The word is nothing. He wants his offering to cost him.

Much is close in feel, but it isn't the word. David says, “…I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” (2 Samuel 24:24). It's nothing that he refuses. He wants an offering that costs him something.

Fifty shekels of silver. The text says, “So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.” (2 Samuel 24:24). The price is stated plain as day. He pays it, and the altar comes next.
Thirty is a little short. The text says David bought the threshing floor and the oxen “for fifty shekels of silver.” (2 Samuel 24:24). Fifty is the number. He pays it himself.
Four hundred would be a big check, friend. The text says David bought the threshing floor and the oxen “for fifty shekels of silver.” (2 Samuel 24:24). Fifty is the number it gives.

Halted is the word. The text says, “Then the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land, and the plague upon Israel was halted.” (2 Samuel 24:25). It stopped. I think that's a long breath out for everybody.

Slowed is close, but the text goes further. It says, “the plague upon Israel was halted.” (2 Samuel 24:25). Halted means it stopped. That happens after the LORD answers the prayers on behalf of the land.
Delayed isn't the word the text uses. It says, “the plague upon Israel was halted.” (2 Samuel 24:25). Halted means it stopped. The LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land.
